A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ASEntmax research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison after matching relocated and renumbered content. Internal numerical inconsistencies limit particular result interpretations but do not prevent identifying the revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-task results, representation and gradient experiments, and attention-scaling analyses from a 120M-parameter model trained on FineWeb, including results in Appendices C, F, and H.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds 420M-parameter language-model evaluations reporting downstream accuracy, long-context perplexity, and RULER retrieval performance in Section 5.2 and Appendix H.9.

M1.justification: The ASEntmax scaling rule, content-dependent per-head beta/gamma projections, and alpha-entmax transformation are retained (v1 Equations 9–10; v3 Equations 8–9). The hybrid NoPE/ALiBi design also remains. New model configurations and NAPE's changed contribution status do not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: v3 adds DCLM-Edu training and evaluation on LAMBADA, HellaSwag, PIQA, ARC-C, WinoGrande, OpenBookQA, The Pile's ArXiv/PubMed subsets, and RULER S-NIAH-1/2. This substantially expands coverage beyond the retained synthetic tasks and FineWeb scaling analysis into natural-text modeling and retrieval.

E2.justification: v3 newly evaluates Top-K attention on Max Retrieval, MQMTAR, Copy, Reverse, and Sort, and Stick-Breaking Attention on the latter four tasks. The MQMTAR comparison drops SEntmax (v1 Table 6; v3 Table 9), although it remains in other comparisons. RoPE comparisons omitted from the main table remain in the appendix.

E3.justification: The added language-model protocol uses 420M-parameter models trained for 7B tokens at length 2048, with evaluation extending to 16K, 500 documents per long-text dataset, and 500 RULER samples per length. Appendix G.3 specifies exponential ALiBi slopes and RoPE testing with a 500,000 base frequency. The retained scaler-fit analysis also changes its logarithmic control from beta log n to delta + beta log n.

E4.justification: New Tables 16–17 compare NAPE, RoPE, and RoPE with adjusted base frequency, testing extrapolation robustness alongside short-context costs. Appendix H adds Top-K sensitivity comparisons, including fixed and length-dependent K on Reverse, while Section 4.1 revises the scaler-fit analysis. Existing representation, gradient, alpha/gamma, RoPE-scaling, and attention-map analyses largely remain.

E5.justification: Both versions' Appendix G.2 reports the single best synthetic model selected across three random seeds and various learning rates. v3 introduces no additional run-count or uncertainty-reporting practice for its language-model results. Confidence intervals, standard deviations, and significance tests are not newly supplied.

E6.justification: The MQMTAR tables change reported NAPE accuracy at 65K from 76.7% to 95.3% for ASEntmax and from 1.0% to 26.7% for SSMax (v1 Table 6; v3 Table 9), without explaining the update history. Numerous comparator and language-model results are added, including ASEntmax's 10.77 ArXiv perplexity and 97.4% S-NIAH-1 accuracy at 16K. Some v3 MQMTAR entries disagree between Tables 1 and 9, limiting precise comparisons.

T1.justification: v3's consolidated Proposition 2 replaces v1's main-text preservation bound 'for any constant c > 0' with existence of a positive constant, matching the earlier appendix's quantification, and explicitly states bounded-support assumptions. The detailed counterexamples and proofs are otherwise retained after the Appendix C/D exchange. This is a localized formal refinement.

C1.justification: v1 presents NAPE as an introduced contribution; v3 explicitly treats it as a practical default rather than a contribution. The abstract and conclusion also broaden the central empirical claims to preserving short-context performance and achieving language-model extrapolation at eight times training length, beyond the retained synthetic extrapolation claims.

C2.justification: Sections 5.2 and H.9 add substantive applicability qualifications concerning near-random downstream performance, PubMed degradation at eightfold extrapolation, and difficult retrieval settings. They interpret RoPE base-frequency adjustment's short-context costs as supporting NAPE's robustness. The conclusion replaces v1's explicit multi-phase, production-scale validation caveat with more optimistic extrapolation from the 420M experiments.

D1.justification: New Appendix G.3 documents language-model dimensions, layers, heads, torchtitan, tokenizer, optimizer, training steps, warm-up/cooldown, learning rates, batch size, and precision. v3 also adds a reproducibility statement explicitly naming FlashAttention-2 and changes the advertised code reference from bigfish to asentmax. These are substantial additions to the documented reproduction setup.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds an attention-scaling discussion covering YaRN, InfoScale, and Scale-invariant Attention, and expands positioning around KERPLE, FIRE, Stick-Breaking, Top-K, and chunk-based attention. NAPE is explicitly connected to Hard-ALiBi's zero-slope configuration instead of claimed as novel. Publication updates to retained works do not constitute new research coverage.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the narrative: it refocuses the abstract and conclusion, consolidates Section 3.3, folds the standalone NAPE section into experimental setup and positioning, divides experiments into synthetic and language-model subsections, and exchanges Appendices C and D. Expanded related work, a reproducibility statement, and an AI-assistant disclosure accompany these structural revisions.

P2.justification: Five language-model tables are added and Table 1 is rebuilt with new comparator rows and without its RoPE blocks. Figure 1 replaces the Reverse panel with the previously separate Max Retrieval comparison, and the scaler-fit figure is redrawn. The redundant main-text representation/gradient figure disappears while its appendix evidence remains. Typography, running headers, and figure/table placement also change throughout.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's limited direct evidence for natural-text applications: the earlier FineWeb experiment analyzed scaling parameters, whereas Section 5.2 and Tables 2–4 and 16–17 directly evaluate language modeling, retrieval, and extrapolation tradeoffs. Added sparse comparators and withdrawal of the NAPE novelty claim strengthen the paper's support and positioning. Reporting problems temper these gains: for example, Top-K MQMTAR accuracy at fourfold length is 6.2% in Table 1 but 99.9% in Table 9, and uncertainty reporting remains limited. These issues weaken exact margins without outweighing the broader empirical improvement.
